name: Sillery Gaon
tagline: A ridge village above Pedong looking down on the Teesta bends
summary: Sillery Gaon is a small homestay village at about 1,830 m above Pedong, roughly 30 km from Kalimpong. Go for Kanchenjunga views, the walk to Ramitey Dara over the bends of the Teesta, and Lepcha history at Damsang Fort. One or two nights is right.
meta_description: Sillery Gaon guide: Ramitey Dara Teesta view, Damsang Fort, Pedong monastery, homestays, how to reach from Kalimpong, costs and best months.
intro: Sillery Gaon is a village of a few dozen houses on a forested ridge at about 1,830 m, a short climb above Pedong. It is about 30 km from Kalimpong and close to the border with East Sikkim. On clear days Kanchenjunga and its neighbours fill the skyline to the north-west.

The village became known to travellers only in the last two decades, when families began opening homestays. Cinchona, planted under the British as a source of quinine, still grows on the slopes. From the ridge above the village, at Ramitey Dara, the Teesta can be seen winding through a long series of bends far below.

Around Sillery lies the oldest history in the district. The ruins of Damsang Fort, the seat of the Lepcha king Gaeboo Achyuk, stand on a ridge near Pedong, and Pedong's Sangchen Dorjee monastery dates from the Bhutanese period. The old trade route to Tibet over Jelep La passed just below.

highlights.title: Ramitey Dara view
highlights.text: A ridge above the village where you look down on the Teesta curling through the valley in many bends.

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga from the village
highlights.text: Many homestays face the snow peaks across the valleys, best from October to February.

highlights.title: Damsang Fort
highlights.text: Ruins of the late seventeenth-century fort of Gaeboo Achyuk, the last Lepcha king of these hills.

highlights.title: Sangchen Dorjee monastery at Pedong
highlights.text: An old monastery built during Bhutanese rule, with wall paintings and a quiet courtyard.

highlights.title: Old Silk Route link
highlights.text: The road on through Rhenock leads to Zuluk and the old Jelep La trade route in East Sikkim.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep from the Kalimpong motor stand to Pedong for about ₹70–120 a seat, about 1–1.5 hours. From Pedong, hire a local jeep for the last steep stretch up to Sillery Gaon for about ₹500–800.

A reserved car from Kalimpong costs about ₹1,800–2,500 and takes about 1.5 hours. From NJP or Bagdogra expect about ₹4,000–5,000 and 3.5–4 hours. The last few kilometres above Pedong are narrow and rough; large vehicles may not make it.
Sillery Gaon is a short drive from Rhenock in East Sikkim, so it fits easily into an Old Silk Route trip towards Aritar or Zuluk.

where_to_stay: Sillery Gaon has only family homestays, many with balconies facing the mountains. Expect about ₹1,500–2,200 a person a night with all meals, indicative. Rooms vary from simple to newly built, so ask for recent photos. Pedong, a few kilometres below, has a few basic lodges if the village is full.
tips: Ask your host whether your car can reach the homestay; the last stretch is steep and narrow.
Walk to Ramitey Dara in the morning, before haze settles over the Teesta valley.
Combine with Pedong, Damsang Fort and the Sangchen Dorjee monastery on the way in or out.
Carry cash; there are no ATMs in the village and few in Pedong.
In the monsoon the road above Pedong turns slippery; travel in daylight and check current status before you travel.

story.title: Gaeboo Achyuk and the fort at Damsang
paras: Long before Kalimpong was a town, the hills around Pedong belonged to a Lepcha kingdom with its seat at Damsang. Its best-remembered ruler was Gaeboo Achyuk, also written Gyalpo Ajok, who lived in the late seventeenth century. Lepchas remember him as a king who united their people across a wide stretch of the hills.

His kingdom sat between powerful neighbours. Achyuk allied with Tibet against Bhutan, and in a war in the late 1670s he captured a Bhutanese outpost at Dalingkot. The Bhutanese took it back and later executed him. After that, the Kalimpong hills came under Bhutanese rule, which lasted until the British annexed them in 1865.

The stone ruins of his fort still stand on a ridge near Pedong. Local stories say spirits helped carry the great round stones up from the Reshi river, that tunnels and treasure lie hidden beneath, and that Bhutanese visitors once feared the place. These are tales handed down over generations, told with relish by local guides.

Every year on 20 December, Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim gather at Damsang to mark Gaeboo Achyuk's birthday with prayers, speeches and songs. From Sillery Gaon the fort is a short drive and walk away.

faqs.q: How do I reach Sillery Gaon from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Drive about 30 km via Algarah and Pedong, around 1.5 hours. A reserved car costs about ₹1,800–2,500, indicative. On a budget, take a shared jeep to Pedong for about ₹70–120 and a local jeep up the last steep stretch for ₹500–800. Ask your homestay to arrange the Pedong pickup.

faqs.q: What is Ramitey Dara?
faqs.a: Ramitey Dara is a viewpoint on the ridge above Sillery Gaon. From the top you look far down on the Teesta as it winds through the valley in a long series of bends; locals count anywhere from 11 to 14. On clear days the snow peaks of Sikkim stand behind. It is about 3 km from the village.

faqs.q: How many nights should I spend in Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: One night is enough for the mountain view, Ramitey Dara and a stop in Pedong. Two nights let you add Damsang Fort, nearby Icche Gaon and a slow day in the village. Many travellers add Sillery Gaon to a Kalimpong stay or use it as the first stop on an Old Silk Route trip.

faqs.q: Why is it called Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: Gaon means village in Nepali. The first part is usually said to come from sillery, a plant that grows in abundance on these slopes, though there are other local stories about the name. Some travel writers have also nicknamed it new Darjeeling, but it is a small farming village with homestays, far quieter than any town.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. Many homestays face the mountains, and the view is wider from Ramitey Dara. October to February gives the best chance, especially early in the morning. In spring haze can hide the peaks after mid-morning, and in the monsoon they are rarely visible.

faqs.q: Is the road to Sillery Gaon good?
faqs.a: The road from Kalimpong to Pedong is reasonable. The last few kilometres from Pedong up to the village are narrow, steep and rough in places, and slippery after rain. Small cars and local jeeps manage; large vehicles may not. Check with your host before travelling, especially in the monsoon.

faqs.q: What else is there to see near Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: Pedong has the old Sangchen Dorjee monastery and a busy little bazaar. Damsang Fort, the ruined seat of the Lepcha king Gaeboo Achyuk, is nearby. Icche Gaon, another homestay village, is a short drive away. Rhenock and Aritar in East Sikkim are about an hour away by road.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: No. Sillery Gaon is in Kalimpong district, West Bengal, and needs no permit for Indians or foreigners. If you continue into East Sikkim via Rhenock towards Aritar or Zuluk, foreigners need a Sikkim permit and Zuluk needs a protected area permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Sillery Gaon good in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, winter is one of the best times, with clear skies and good mountain views from November to February. Nights drop to a few degrees above freezing, and houses are not heated, so bring thermals and a warm hat. Lepchas gather at nearby Damsang Fort on 20 December each year.

experiences.title: Walk to Ramitey Dara above the Teesta
experiences.summary: Walk or ride about 3 km from Sillery Gaon to Ramitey Dara, where the Teesta can be seen winding through the valley in many bends.
body: The path to Ramitey Dara climbs gently through forest and small clearings above the village. At the top an open ridge looks down on the Teesta valley, with the river curling back and forth on its way south. Locals count anywhere from 11 to 14 bends; on a clear morning you can trace it for many kilometres.
Behind the river the hills of Sikkim rise in layers, and on the best days the snow peaks line the far horizon. Morning is clearest; by afternoon haze often fills the valley.
Some homestays arrange a jeep for part of the way; walking is more enjoyable in dry weather.

faqs.q: How far is Ramitey Dara from Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: It is about 3 km from the village, roughly an hour's walk each way at an easy pace. Part of the route can be done by jeep if you prefer. The path is mostly gentle, with a few steeper bits near the top. Ask your host to point out the start or send someone with you.

faqs.q: How many bends of the Teesta can I see from Ramitey Dara?
faqs.a: Locals and guidebooks give different numbers, usually between 11 and 14, depending on how you count and how clear the day is. What matters is the view: the river looping back on itself far below, with the hills of Sikkim behind. Go in the morning for the clearest air.

faqs.q: Is Ramitey Dara worth it in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Usually not. From June to September the valley is often filled with cloud and the path is slippery and full of leeches. You may get brief gaps, but the view is often hidden. Go between October and May, ideally from October to February.

experiences.title: Damsang Fort, seat of the last Lepcha king
experiences.summary: Visit the ruins of Damsang Fort near Pedong, linked to the Lepcha king Gaeboo Achyuk, with a local guide who knows the stories.
body: Damsang Fort, often called Damsang Gadi, stands on a forested ridge between Pedong and Algarah. Only sections of rough stone walls survive among the trees, but the site is important to Lepchas as the seat of Gaeboo Achyuk, who ruled in the late seventeenth century and was later executed by the Bhutanese.

A local guide brings the place to life with stories of the king, the stones carried up from the river and the tunnels said to run beneath. On 20 December each year Lepchas gather here to mark his birthday.
The approach is a rough road and a short walk; wear sturdy shoes.
experiences.best_time: October to May, or 20 December for the Lepcha gathering.
experiences.cost: ₹1,200–2,000 per jeep for a half-day tour

faqs.q: How old is Damsang Fort?
faqs.a: Local tradition dates the fort to around 1690, built by the Lepcha king Gaeboo Achyuk to resist the Bhutanese. Historians link Achyuk to wars in the 1670s, so the fort belongs to the late seventeenth century. Only ruins remain, but the site is still central to Lepcha history and identity.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Damsang Fort?
faqs.a: There is usually no formal ticket. You pay for the jeep and, if you want one, a local guide. Treat the site with respect: do not climb on fragile walls or remove stones, and do not leave litter. Arrangements can change, so ask your homestay host before you go.

faqs.q: Can I combine Damsang Fort with Pedong?
faqs.a: Yes, they make a good half-day together. Visit the Sangchen Dorjee monastery and Pedong bazaar, then drive towards Algarah for the fort. A jeep tour from Sillery Gaon costs about ₹1,200–2,000, indicative. Add Icche Gaon if you have time.

experiences.title: Pedong and the Sangchen Dorjee monastery
experiences.summary: Stop in Pedong bazaar and visit the Sangchen Dorjee monastery, built during Bhutanese rule over these hills.
body: Pedong is a small market town on the old trade route to Tibet, a short drive below Sillery Gaon. Its oldest building is the Sangchen Dorjee monastery, built in the early eighteenth century when Bhutan ruled the Kalimpong hills. Its wall paintings and quiet courtyard are worth a slow look.
Pedong also has a bazaar where villagers shop, a few momo stalls and views towards Sikkim across the valley. It is a natural stop on the way to or from Sillery Gaon.
Dress modestly in the monastery, remove shoes before entering and ask before taking photographs.

faqs.q: How old is the Sangchen Dorjee monastery?
faqs.a: It was built during Bhutanese rule over the Kalimpong hills and is usually dated to the early eighteenth century, around 1706, making it one of the oldest monasteries in the district. Accounts of the exact year vary. Ask the caretaker monk for its story when you visit.

faqs.q: Is Pedong worth a stop?
faqs.a: Yes, especially on the way to Sillery Gaon or the Old Silk Route. Pedong has the old monastery, a small bazaar and views over the valley towards Sikkim. You can see it in an hour or two. It also has basic lodges if Sillery Gaon is full.

faqs.q: How far is Pedong from Sillery Gaon?
faqs.a: Pedong is a few kilometres below Sillery Gaon, about 20–30 minutes by jeep on a narrow road. Most visitors pass through on the way in or out. Shared jeeps run from Kalimpong to Pedong; local jeeps cover the last stretch up to Sillery.

experiences.title: Farm morning and home cooking in Sillery
experiences.summary: Spend a morning with your homestay family in the kitchen garden and kitchen, learning to cook local greens, dal and momos.
body: Most Sillery Gaon families grow some of what they cook: greens, beans, squash, potatoes, chillies and herbs in small terraced plots. A morning with your host might start with picking vegetables and end at the stove.

You might learn how to cook saag with garlic, make a simple dal, fold momos or prepare a tomato and chilli achar. Lunch is what you cooked. It is informal, and the point is time with the family rather than a polished class.
Agree any extra charge in advance and tell your host about dietary needs.
experiences.cost: Often included; some hosts ask ₹300–500 extra

faqs.q: Do all Sillery Gaon homestays offer cooking sessions?
faqs.a: Not formally. Most families are happy for guests to watch or help in the kitchen if asked, but few run set classes. Ask when you book, and agree any extra charge. The experience is relaxed and depends on the family's day, so be flexible.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food easy to get?
faqs.a: Yes. Home meals are built around rice, dal, vegetables and greens, with eggs or chicken added for those who eat them. Tell your host you are vegetarian when you book, and they will cook accordingly. Vegan food is possible but mention dairy and ghee clearly.

faqs.q: What local foods should I try?
faqs.a: Try saag, local greens cooked with garlic; gundruk, fermented leafy greens; squash and potato curries; tomato and chilli achar; momos; and churpi, a hard cheese. In season, look for local oranges and fresh ginger. Ask your host about dishes their family makes for festivals.
